headline: The Pharmacy & Traveler Health Foundation
threshold: By Lesson 10, you can greet a pharmacist, say how you feel and what you need, ask about prices, times and labels, ask for help politely, and start Pharmacy & Traveler Health Lesson 1.

lessons.title: Sounds and Greetings
lessons.objective: Greet a pharmacist politely and say basic pharmacy words with clear Spanish sounds.
lessons.focus: the five vowels, ch, j, ll, rr and the written accent; greetings

words.note: Stress on -ma-: far-MA-sia. In Latin America, c before i sounds like s.
The accent marks the stress: far-ma-CÉU-ti-co. A woman is la farmacéutica.
ll sounds like English y: pas-TI-ya.
j is a strong h sound: ha-RA-be.
rr is a rolled r. Catarro is a common word for a head cold.
ch sounds like church. The accent puts the stress on -pú.
The accent marks the stress: CLÍ-ni-ca.
People also say el doctor. A woman is la médica or la doctora.

words.en: Good afternoon, my name is Alex.
words.note: Use buenas tardes from noon until dark.
Formal: use usted with pharmacists and clinic staff.

words.en: Thank you very much, see you later.

lessons.speaking: Greet the pharmacist, say your name, ask how they are, and say three pharmacy words clearly.

lessons.title: Numbers, Time and Measurements
lessons.objective: Understand prices, opening times and package quantities at a pharmacy.
lessons.focus: numbers 0 to 1,000, clock time, pesos, and package units like boxes, capsules, mg and mL

words.note: A small bottle, as for syrup or pills.
A small packet of powder, such as oral rehydration salts.
Written mg on labels.
Written mL on labels.
Mexican prices are written with the $ sign.
Without the article, mañana means tomorrow.
Use es la for 1 o'clock: Es la 1.

words.en: The label says there are 20 capsules.
words.es: La etiqueta dice que hay 20 cápsulas.

words.en: The label says 500 mg per capsule.
words.es: La etiqueta dice 500 mg por cápsula.

lessons.speaking: Ask the pharmacist how much a box costs, repeat the price in pesos, and ask what time the pharmacy closes.

lessons.title: Ser and Estar
lessons.objective: Say who you are, how you feel, and whether a pharmacy is open or near.
lessons.focus: ser for what someone or something is, estar for feelings, conditions and location

words.note: A woman says enferma.
A woman says mareada.
A woman says cansada.
Use with ser: soy alérgico. A woman says alérgica.
Use with estar. La farmacia está abierta.
Use with estar. La clínica está cerrada.

words.en: I'm a tourist from the United States.
words.note: ser: who you are.
ser for a lasting trait. A man says alérgico.
estar: a condition that can change. A woman says mareada.

words.en: The clinic is near the hotel.
words.es: La clínica está cerca del hotel.
words.note: estar for location. de + el becomes del.

lessons.speaking: Tell the pharmacist you are a tourist, say how you feel today, and ask if a clinic is near or far.

lessons.title: Have, There Is, Need and Want
lessons.objective: Say your symptoms and what you need or want to buy at a pharmacy.
lessons.focus: tener, hay, necesitar, querer and hay que + infinitive

words.note: Mexico. A small adhesive bandage, like a Band-Aid.
Common in Mexico. People also say el protector solar.
Spanish uses tener for symptoms: tengo fiebre, tengo tos.

words.en: Is there a pharmacy around here?
words.note: hay means there is or there are.

words.en: I need bandages for a blister.

words.es: Quiero un bloqueador solar, por favor.

words.en: You have to read the label first.
words.es: Hay que leer la etiqueta primero.
words.note: hay que + infinitive: something everyone has to do.

lessons.speaking: Tell the pharmacist two symptoms you have, say what you need, and ask if there is a sunscreen.

lessons.title: Go, Do and Can
lessons.objective: Say where you are going, make plans for appointments, and ask what you can do.
lessons.focus: ir and ir a + infinitive for plans, hacer, and poder to ask permission

words.note: The h is silent: os-pi-TAL.
A woman is la dentista.
Mexico. In other countries people also say los anteojos.

words.en: I'm going to the hospital by taxi.
words.note: a + el becomes al.

words.en: Tomorrow I'm going to go to the optician's.
words.es: Mañana voy a ir a la óptica.

words.en: Can I make an appointment for today?
words.note: People say hacer una cita for making an appointment.

words.en: This afternoon we're going to the airport.

lessons.speaking: Tell the receptionist where you are going today, ask if you can make an appointment, and ask if you can wait there.

lessons.title: Present Tense
lessons.objective: Talk about what you take, use, eat and drink, and about your trip.
lessons.focus: present tense of regular -ar, -er, -ir verbs for yo, tú, usted, nosotros and ellos

words.note: Agua is feminine but takes el: el agua fría.

words.en: I take a vitamin with breakfast.
words.es: Tomo una vitamina con el desayuno.
words.note: tomar: to take medicine, and to drink.

words.en: I use an inhaler at night.
words.es: Uso un inhalador en la noche.
words.note: Mexico says en la noche. Spain says por la noche.
Informal tú: with a travel companion or a friend.
Formal usted: with the pharmacist.

lessons.speaking: Tell the pharmacist what medicine or vitamin you take, how long your trip is, and ask if they sell eye drops.

lessons.title: Questions
lessons.objective: Ask where, when, who and how at a pharmacy or clinic.
lessons.focus: question words qué, quién, dónde, cuándo, cuánto, cómo, por qué, cuál

words.note: For things you count, use ¿cuántos? or ¿cuántas?
A plain ¿Cómo? also asks someone to repeat.
Two words with an accent. Porque, one word, means because.

words.en: When does the doctor's office open?
What are the clinic's opening hours?
words.es: ¿Cuál es el horario de la clínica?
words.note: Use ¿cuál es? before a noun like horario or nombre.

words.en: How do you use this cream?

lessons.speaking: Ask a clinic receptionist when they open, who speaks English, and what the label on your medicine says.

lessons.title: No, Never and How Much
lessons.objective: Say what you don't have yet, decline extras, and ask for another option.
lessons.focus: no, nunca, nadie, nada, todavía no, más, menos and otro

words.note: Spanish uses a double negative: No quiero nada.
Never say un otro. Use otro or otra alone.
Short for el medicamento genérico.

words.en: There's nobody at the front desk.
words.es: No hay nadie en la recepción.

words.en: I don't have an appointment yet.
Do you have a cheaper one?
I don't want anything else, thanks.

lessons.speaking: Tell the pharmacist you don't have a prescription yet, ask for another brand or size, and politely decline anything else.

lessons.title: Polite Requests and Commands
lessons.objective: Politely ask staff to repeat, explain, write or wait.
lessons.focus: ¿Puede…? for polite requests and usted commands for everyday verbs

words.note: In Mexico, a formal invoice. Ask for one if your insurance needs it.
Means address, not direction.

words.en: Can you give me an invoice for my insurance?
words.es: ¿Me puede dar una factura para el seguro?
Escriba la dirección aquí, por favor.
words.note: Usted command: -ar verbs end in -e, -er/-ir verbs in -a.

words.en: Please explain the label to me.
words.note: me attaches to the command and adds an accent.

lessons.speaking: Ask the pharmacist to repeat slowly, explain the label to you, and give you a receipt or invoice for your insurance.

lessons.title: Words You Already Know and Getting Help
lessons.objective: Use cognates and survival phrases to get help fast in an emergency.
lessons.focus: cognates ending in -ción, -dad, -ente and survival phrases for getting help

words.note: -ción words are feminine and match English -tion.
A woman is la paciente.
Área is feminine but takes el. Signs often just say Urgencias.
In Mexico, the Red Cross runs many ambulances.

words.es: Llame a una ambulancia, por favor.
words.note: In Mexico, the emergency number is 911.

words.en: My friend is having an allergic reaction.
words.es: Mi amiga tiene una reacción alérgica.
words.note: A male friend is mi amigo.

lessons.speaking: Tell a pharmacist it is an emergency, say your friend has an allergic reaction, and ask them to call an ambulance.
